cta_hook: Scams run on panic. So does ignoring your body.

caption:
The scariest part is how calm the caller sounds.

Pennsylvania State Police issued a warning about a scam that has taken an estimated $6.5 million. Victims across several states, including Maryland and Washington, have been hit. Two people were arrested after a traffic stop on Interstate 80 on September 10, 2026.

How it works, according to police:

1. It starts with fear
A computer pop-up or a call from someone posing as a federal agent says your identity or bank accounts are tied to a crime.

2. Then comes the ask
You're told to withdraw cash, buy gold, and hand it to a courier, supposedly to protect it.

3. Then it's gone
The "courier" is part of the scam. Once the gold or cash is handed over, it's gone.

What police say every time: no legitimate law enforcement officer will tell you to buy gold or give cash or gold to a courier. Montgomery County police describe the calls as run by organized call centers overseas, and police in Shelton, Connecticut say seniors are being targeted.

(Sources: Pennsylvania State Police, Shelton CT police, Montgomery County MD police.)

If this happens to someone you love: tell them to hang up, call a family member, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If gold or cash has already been handed over, call local police right away.

I can recognize a scam from the first sentence now. For years I never paid the same attention to my body.

We know how to spot a scam. Almost nobody teaches us how to spot our own body's warning signs. I put them in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.

They need you scared and in a hurry. I'd never thought about how my own body does the same thing.

cta_hook: Panic is how they get you. Slowing down is how you win.
cta_bridge: We know how to spot a scam. Almost nobody teaches us how to spot our body's warning signs.
caption:
The caller always stays on the line. That's not an accident.

Police departments in several cities have warned about a jury duty scam again this month. A caller says you missed jury duty, there's a warrant, and you can avoid arrest by paying a fine right now.

How it works:

1. They pose as court staff or officers
Sheriff's deputies, court clerks, even federal officers.

2. They demand payment fast
Gift cards, payment apps, cryptocurrency or cash. Some ask you to photograph the cards, or mail them to a clerk's office to seem legitimate.

3. They keep you on the phone
If you stay on the line, you can't stop and think, and you can't call anyone.

What real courts do: they send jury summonses by mail. They don't demand payment by phone, email, gift card or cryptocurrency. Your caller ID may show a real courthouse number, but scammers can fake it.

(Sources: county clerk and state consumer-protection offices in Wisconsin and Nebraska; local police alerts.)

If you get the call: hang up, don't pay anything, and call the court clerk using the number from the court's official website. If you've already paid, contact your bank, payment app or the gift card company immediately, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

I thought scams only worked on people who weren't careful. It's the opposite. They work on careful people who are scared.

We know how to read a scam. I learned to read my body's signals too, and put it all in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.

cta_bridge: We know how to spot a scam. Almost nobody teaches us how to spot our body's warning signs.
caption:
You may really be expecting a package. That's why it works.

Police and attorneys general keep warning about the "FedEx" text scam. A text says a package couldn't be delivered and gives you a tracking code and a link to reschedule.

What the warnings say:

1. The link is the trap
In the FTC's account, it leads to a page posing as a customer survey that offers a prize, then asks for a credit card number to cover "shipping and handling." Some versions sign you up for expensive services.

2. FedEx says it didn't send it
FedEx says it doesn't send unsolicited texts or emails asking for money, packages or personal information.

3. Other carriers get used too
Scammers also pretend to be UPS, USPS and Amazon, so a text naming another carrier can be the same scheme.

(Sources: FTC consumer alert; Idaho and Florida attorneys general; FedEx guidance. Most of these warnings date from 2020 to 2022, so check FedEx's current page for the latest advice.)

What to do: delete the text without opening the link. If you're expecting something, type the tracking number directly into FedEx's website. If it isn't recognized, it isn't real. You can forward the message to abuse@fedex.com.

I've been the person who tapped first and thought later. It's easy to do when you're busy.

caption:
The editors didn't talk about fear. They talked about habits.

The Points Guy asked its editors who travel alone for the small things they always do. None of it needs special gear or a big budget.

What they said:

1. Don't advertise that you're solo
One editor, Olivia Mittak, tells people she's meeting friends. She also writes down her hotel room number rather than saying it out loud when asked.

2. Be firm
Another, Lyndsey Matthews, says a strong, polite "no, thank you" works when someone seems to be scamming you or something feels unsafe.

3. Make a safety net
Annie Black tells any friends at her destination that she's visiting, even if she barely knows them. Several editors share their location through apps like Find My, and carry local cash for cash-only shops or broken ATMs.

(Source: The Points Guy, "solo travel safety tips." The article is the editors' own advice, not research.)

None of this is about being afraid of the world, and none of it makes you paranoid. You don't need to be fearful to be careful. The point of these habits is that they take almost no effort, and they make you a harder target by default.

On every trip I noticed the same thing. I planned carefully for strangers, taxis and hotels. I never planned for my own body: sleep, swelling, energy, what the flight did to me.

Every trip taught me something about how a woman's body changes after 40. I wrote it down and put it in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.

caption:
It isn't the laundry. It's the water that leaves it.

In winter a lot of us dry clothes indoors: on the radiator, on a rack, over a door. It feels like the thrifty choice. But as clothes dry, the water in them has to go somewhere.

What I found in consumer and health coverage:

1. It adds up
Several sources say one load of laundry puts about 2 liters of water into your indoor air as it dries.

2. Damp invites mould
One article quoting experts says mould can spread when indoor humidity stays above about 60%.

3. Some people feel it more
Asthma charities say damp air and mould spores can trigger or worsen asthma in people sensitive to them. Dust mites also increase in humid conditions.

The honest limits: these figures come mostly from consumer and appliance-company articles and expert quotes, not from one big study. I couldn't confirm them against the World Health Organization's dampness and mould guidance, so treat the numbers as rough.

(Sources: Onmanorama, Meaco, Ebac and Quotezone coverage of indoor drying; asthma charity guidance quoted in those articles.)

What helps: open a window, use a dehumidifier if you have one, and dry outside when you can. If you have asthma, ask your doctor what to do about damp air in your home.

I'd worried about mould on the walls for years. It never crossed my mind to ask what the air in my own home was doing to my sleep and breathing.

caption:
It tasted the same. That was the whole plan.

For decades, McDonald's french fries were cooked in a blend that was mostly beef tallow. Tallow has a high smoke point, and at the time it was cheaper than vegetable oil. It's a big part of why the fries tasted the way people remember.

What happened next:

1. 1990: the switch
McDonald's announced it would move to 100% vegetable oil. Several accounts link the change to pressure from health advocates, though the company has never said so definitively.

2. The taste problem
Without tallow, the fries tasted different. The company added natural beef flavoring to the oil to recover some of the original taste.

3. 2007: another change
The company moved again, to a trans-fat-free cooking oil.

The point isn't about one restaurant. It's that a recipe can change while the logo, the box and the memory all stay the same. Most of us checked labels once, years ago, and never looked again.

(Sources: Food Republic, Chowhound, The Takeout and Tasting Table histories of the McDonald's fry. Motives and exact dates vary by account.)

Try this: pick five things you've bought for years and read the ingredient list as if it were new. You may be surprised by what's in them now.

I read labels on new products all the time. I never re-read the ones I'd trusted for decades. It made me wonder what else I'd stopped checking.

I started reading what my body had been trying to tell me, and put it in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.

slides.text: Bronnie Ware spent years in palliative care. She wrote a blog post about the regrets her patients shared.
"I wish I'd had the courage to live a life true to myself, not the life others expected of me."
"I wish I hadn't worked so hard." "I wish I'd stayed in touch with friends."
"I wish I'd let myself be happier." And one about feelings: "I wish I'd had the courage to express them."
I've been waiting for permission to put myself on the list.

cta_hook: Nobody wishes they'd waited longer to take care of themselves.
cta_bridge: "At your age?" Sometimes it's the first time you put yourself on the list.
caption:
She didn't write it for a study. She wrote it because she kept hearing the same thing.

Bronnie Ware, an Australian palliative care nurse, spent years caring for people in their last weeks. She started writing down what they said they regretted most, and published it as a blog post. It was read by more than three million people in its first year and became a memoir, published in 2012.

The five regrets she described:

1. "I wish I'd had the courage to live a life true to myself, not the life others expected of me."

2. "I wish I hadn't worked so hard."

3. "I wish I'd had the courage to express my feelings."

4. "I wish I had stayed in touch with my friends."

5. "I wish I had let myself be happier."

To be clear: this is one nurse's account of what patients told her. It isn't a scientific study. It's a list that moved millions of people because so many of us recognize ourselves in it.

(Source: Bronnie Ware, The Top Five Regrets of the Dying, 2012, and her original blog post.)

Read the list again and notice which one stings. For many women I know it's the first and the last: living for other people's expectations, and putting happiness on hold.

I've spent years taking care of everyone else and calling it love. Taking care of yourself later in life isn't starting too late. Sometimes it's simply the first time you finally put yourself on the list.

I started with my body, because it had been trying to tell me things for years. I wrote down what I found and put it in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.

I thought it would creep up. Maybe the signals start earlier than we're told.

cta_hook: It doesn't have to feel like a cliff. It helps to see it coming.
cta_bridge: I kept thinking it was just aging. It wasn't.
caption:
The word "cliff" got the clicks. The details are more interesting.

On October 12, 2026, researchers from the Weizmann Institute published a study in Nature Medicine on what happens in the body around menopause. They used a computational method on more than 300 million lab tests from over a million women in the US and Israel, from 1999 to 2024.

What they found:

1. Many tests changed abruptly
In the US data, 52 of 90 lab tests, including bone, liver, kidney, blood chemistry and blood fat markers, showed a statistically significant abrupt change.

2. Hormones moved early
Three sex hormones changed more than a decade before the final menstrual period.

3. Hormone therapy was linked to smaller changes
This was observational and needs confirming.

The pushback: Martha Hickey, who heads menopause services and wasn't involved, called the "cliff-like" framing unnecessarily alarming and said it isn't a scientific or medical term. She noted that the established SWAN study suggests these changes are gradual.

The honest limits: this was retrospective lab data, menopause timing was partly self-reported, and experts disagree on how to read it.

(Sources: Nature Medicine, October 2026, as reported by Newsweek, ThePrint and Nature Asia.)

Whichever side is right, change may start years earlier than we expect. Ask your doctor about baseline blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar in your forties.

I spent years thinking it would just creep up and I'd cope. It helps to see it coming. I wrote down what I learned and put it in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.
